from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite Refresher: The Linear Map", [
            "Matrices are functions mapping vectors between spaces.",
            "Square matrices stay in the same dimension.",
            "Non-square matrices change the space dimension."
        ])
        
        # Objects
        v = Arrow(start=ORIGIN, end=RIGHT*1.5, color=WHITE).set_stroke(width=4)
        v_label = Text("v", font_size=24, color=WHITE).next_to(v.get_end(), UP, buff=0.1)
        v_group = VGroup(v, v_label)
        
        av = Arrow(start=ORIGIN, end=UP*1.2+RIGHT*0.5, color="#ADD8E6").set_stroke(width=4)
        av_label = Text("Av", font_size=24, color="#ADD8E6").next_to(av.get_end(), RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        av_group = VGroup(av, av_label)
        
        prop_text = Text("L(u+v) = L(u)+L(v)", font_size=20, color="#90EE90")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(v_group, 'C3')
        self.play(FadeIn(v_group))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#ADD8E6")
        self.play(ReplacementTransform(v_group.copy(), av_group))
        self.play(FadeIn(av_group))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#90EE90")
        self.place_at_grid(prop_text, 'E3')
        self.play(Write(prop_text))
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout(
            "Dimensional Compression (m < n): The Projection", 
            ["Columns greater than rows mean compression.", 
             "High-dimensional data squashes into smaller spaces.", 
             "Depth and detail are lost during projection."]
        )
        
        # 1. 3D volume
        cube = Cube(fill_opacity=0.6, stroke_width=2, color="#FF4500")
        self.place_at_grid(cube, "C3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # 2. 2D target plane
        plane = Square(fill_opacity=0.3, stroke_width=2, color="#FF4500")
        self.place_at_grid(plane, "C3", scale_factor=1.2)
        plane.rotate(PI/4, axis=RIGHT)
        
        # 3. Text
        projection_text = Text("Projection: R^3 -> R^2", font_size=24, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(projection_text, "A3")

        # Animation Sequence
        self.play(Create(cube))
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(1)

        self.play(
            cube.animate.scale([1, 1, 0.01]),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE)
        )
        self.wait(1)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(projection_text), self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: Geometric Interpretation of Non-Square Matrices as Dimensional Transformations

sections.title: Prerequisite Refresher: The Linear Map
sections.content: Briefly define a matrix as a function that maps vectors from one space to another. Remind students that square matrices keep us in the same dimension (e.g., 2D to 2D), while non-square matrices force a change in the 'stage' where the vector lives.
sections.example: Visualizing a 2D plane as a sheet of paper. A square matrix (2x2) rotates or stretches the paper. A non-square matrix (e.g., 3x2) moves the paper into a 3D room.

sections.title: Dimensional Expansion (m > n): The Embedding
sections.content: Explain that when the number of rows > columns, the matrix maps a lower-dimensional space into a higher-dimensional one. It acts like a 'scaffolding' tool, placing a flat object into a larger, empty volume.
sections.example: Imagine a 2D cat character. A 3x2 matrix maps the cat onto a 3D wall. The cat remains 2D, but it now exists within 3D coordinates (the wall has depth).

sections.title: Dimensional Compression (m < n): The Projection
sections.content: Explain the reverse: when columns > rows, the matrix acts as a 'filter' or 'projector'. It squashes higher-dimensional information into a smaller space, losing depth or detail in the process.
sections.example: A 3D robotic arm's position (3D) is mapped to a 2D control screen (2x3). The matrix 'flattens' the arm's complex 3D reach onto the 2D display, showing only the shadow or silhouette.

sections.title: The Null Space: What gets lost?
sections.content: Introduce the concept of 'Information Loss'. When projecting to lower dimensions, multiple points in the higher dimension might map to the same point in the lower dimension. Use this to explain why the transformation isn't always reversible.
sections.example: A 'Magical Flashlight': If you shine a light on a 3D cube (3D) and cast its shadow on a wall (2D), the shadow is a square. You can't tell if the object was a cube or a flat cardboard sheet just by looking at the 2D shadow.

sections.title: Summary & Real-World Application
sections.content: Conclude by unifying the concepts: Linear transformations are about how we interpret data. Dimensionality reduction (compression) is how we simplify complex models (like AI neural networks).
sections.example: Summarize the animation: A 'Dimension-Slider' where the matrix $A$ stretches, twists, and flattens a shape, turning a 2D shape into a 3D object and back to 2D.
